# Variables, strings, and DNA

Chapter 5 read one number off the *BRCA1* record: the coding sequence of
`NM_007294.4` starts at base 114. Hand that 114 to Python and ask for base 114.
You get a `T`. The record says an `A`, and both of them are right.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. The letter that comes back is real sequence
sitting one place along, which is the worst kind of wrong answer there is. So
this chapter is about what Python is holding while it counts, and why it and
the database disagree about where base 114 is.

## A sequence is a string, and that's all it is

A [string]{.term def="An ordered run of characters that a program keeps as one
value. Order matters and the program does not know what the characters mean."}
is an ordered run of characters that Python keeps as one value. The order is
remembered exactly. The meaning is not remembered at all, because there's
nowhere in a string to put it. The same four letters could be DNA or a set of
initials, and nothing inside the string would tell you which.

Look at what DNA is once it's written down. An ordered run of letters, where
the order carries the whole meaning. Same shape as a string, which is why this
book starts you on strings rather than on numbers.

A [variable]{.term def="A name attached to a value, so the value can be used
again by name."} is a name you attach to a value so you can use the value
again. The name goes on the left, an equals sign in the middle, the value on
the right. Nothing is copied and nothing is stored twice. You've made a label.

One habit is worth building right now, on your first variable. Give it a name
that says what the thing is, because in four weeks you'll open this notebook
again and `x` will tell you nothing while `brca1` will tell you everything. A
name can hold letters, digits and the `_` character. It can't start with a
digit, and `Brca1` and `brca1` are two different names.

Type this into a Colab cell. The value is the first 200 bases of `NM_007294.4`,
the human *BRCA1* transcript from Chapter 5, and the last line asks for a count
of the characters it took.

```{python}
brca1 = (
    "GCTGAGACTTCCTGGACGGGGGACAGGCTGTGGGGTTTCTCAGATAACTG"
    "GGCCCCTGCGCTCAGGAGGCCTTCACCCTCTGCTCTGGGTAAAGTTCATT"
    "GGAACAGAAAGAAATGGATTTATCTGCTCTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAA"
    "ATGTCATTAATGCTATGCAGAAAATCTTAGAGTGTCCCATCTGTCTGGAG"
)
print(len(brca1))
```

Four quoted pieces, one variable. Strings that sit side by side inside
parentheses get glued into one, so `brca1` holds a single run of 200 characters
rather than four runs of 50. The split into four lines is a printing decision.
200 characters won't fit across this page, and nothing inside `brca1` remembers
where the breaks were.

<!-- nlr-allow: 200 199 -->

`len()` counts characters. You can check its answer without trusting it: 4
lines times 50 characters is 200.

[Keep this cell. Every code block in this chapter reuses `brca1`, and Colab
forgets your variables when the runtime disconnects.]{.margin}

### Counting bases

`.count()` goes on the end of a string, takes a piece of text, and tells you
how many times that piece appears. Ask it for all four bases at once, so you
can check its answers against a length you already have.

```{python}
print(brca1.count("A"), brca1.count("C"),
      brca1.count("G"), brca1.count("T"))
```

::: {.check}
Add those four numbers: 49 + 43 + 55 + 53 = 200. That's the same 200 that
`len(brca1)` printed. If your four counts add up to less than the length, your
string holds something that isn't a base, and an `N` or a stray space is the
usual culprit.
:::

Now a number you work out from the sequence itself rather than read off a
record. GC content is the fraction of a sequence that's G or C, and you get it
by counting two letters and dividing by the length.

```{python}
gc = brca1.count("G") + brca1.count("C")
print(gc, gc / len(brca1))
```

98 bases out of 200, which is 0.49. Just under half of this stretch is G or C.

::: {.why}
G pairs with C across three hydrogen bonds. A pairs with T across two. So a
GC-rich stretch of DNA takes more heat to pull apart than an AT-rich one. Every
experiment that heats DNA to separate the strands runs into this, which is why
GC content is on the front page of so many tools. It also varies along a
transcript, and you'll see that for yourself in Exercise 11.1.
:::

### The same sequence in lowercase counts as zero

Sequence doesn't always arrive in capitals. NCBI's GenBank flatfile view prints
the sequence at the bottom in lowercase, and plenty of genome files use
lowercase to mark regions that repeat. To a string, `g` and `G` are two
unrelated characters with nothing in common.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the GenBank flatfile view of `NM_007294.4` on 2 August 2026.
The sequence at the foot of that page is printed in lowercase.
:::

`.upper()` hands back an all-capitals copy of a string and `.lower()` hands
back a lowercase one. Neither one changes the string you called it on. Make a
lowercase copy of your own sequence and count it, so you meet this problem on a
string whose right answer you already know.

```{python}
lowercase = brca1.lower()
print(lowercase.count("G") + lowercase.count("C"))
print(lowercase.upper().count("G") + lowercase.upper().count("C"))
```

::: {.trap}
That first line printed 0, and it was right to. There's no capital `G` anywhere
in `lowercase`, so the honest count is zero. You know that zero is wrong only
because you counted 98 a moment ago, and it arrives with no error message, no
warning and no red text. The second line goes through `.upper()` first and gets
the 98 back. So call `.upper()` on any sequence the moment it enters your
notebook, before you count anything at all.
:::

## The numbers label the gaps, not the letters

Slow down for this section. It's the piece of the chapter that costs people
whole evenings, and it takes them quietly.

You'd expect a position number to name a letter. These ones don't. They name
the spaces between the letters instead, and the counting starts at the space in
front of the first letter. Here are the first six bases of `brca1` with the
gaps numbered.

``` {.default}
     G   C   T   G   A   G
    0   1   2   3   4   5   6
```

Gap 0 sits before everything and gap 6 sits after everything. Six letters give
you seven gaps, and that one extra number is the whole story of this chapter.

`brca1[0]` means "the letter just after gap 0", which is `G`. `brca1[1]` is the
letter after gap 1, which is `C`. Python isn't counting from zero because
somebody picked a convention to annoy you. It's counting gaps, and there really
is a gap before the first letter.

A [slice]{.term def="A run of characters cut out of a string, written
name[start:end]. The end number is a gap, so that letter is not included."} is
written with two gap numbers and a colon between them. `brca1[2:5]` means
"everything between gap 2 and gap 5".

```{python}
print(brca1[2:5], len(brca1[2:5]))
```

Read that straight off the diagram. Gap 2 sits before `T`, gap 5 sits after
`A`, and what lies between the two of them is `TGA`. Three letters, and 5 minus
2 is 3.

That subtraction works whenever both numbers land inside the string. The length
of a Python slice is the end number minus the start number, with no plus one to
remember. Ask for an end past the last gap and Python hands back whatever
exists rather than complaining. That's the one case where the subtraction
promises more than you get. Once you're thinking in gaps you can stop
memorizing the rule and redo the arithmetic instead.

There's a second thing the gap model gives you free. Two slices that share a
number sit flush against each other with nothing missing and nothing repeated,
so `brca1[0:50]` and `brca1[50:100]` between them cover the first hundred bases
exactly once. That's why the windows in Chapter 12 can walk a sequence in steps
of 100 without counting any base twice.

### The other system, which is also correct

Genome browsers don't work this way, and GenBank doesn't either. Chapter 5's
"base 114 to base 5,705" came off a GenBank record, and so does almost every
coordinate anybody will ever hand you. Those systems number the letters
themselves, the count starts at 1, and a range includes both of its ends.

Take the same six bases. In that system letter 1 is `G` and letter 6 is the
second `G`. The range 3 to 5 covers `T`, `G` and `A`.

Both systems have now described the same three letters. One called it `[2:5]`
and the other called it 3 to 5. Neither is a mistake, neither is going away,
and you'll use both of them in the same afternoon for the rest of your working
life. The two counting systems disagree because they were built for different
jobs. Python's job is cutting pieces out of a run of characters. The record's
job is telling a person which base you mean.

The dangerous part is that they overlap. Feed a 1-based number to a program
that wants a 0-based one and you don't get an error, because the wrong number
is a perfectly legal position. You get a base, and the base you get is the one
next door.

Two rules carry you across, and they're worth writing on something you keep
near the keyboard.

1. A 1-based position becomes a Python index by subtracting 1.
2. A 1-based inclusive range `start..stop` becomes the Python slice
   `[start - 1 : stop]`. The start moves. The stop doesn't.

The second one looks lopsided and people distrust it on sight. It's the gaps
again. Gap number `stop` sits immediately after letter `stop`, so writing
`stop` as the end of a slice takes that letter with you instead of cutting it
off. Do the two conversions separately and check each one, rather than trying
to fix the pair with a single adjustment at the end.

<!-- nlr-allow: 113 114 152 -->

## Walkthrough: pulling out a coding sequence by its coordinates

Back to the 114 from the top of this chapter. The record gives the coding
sequence of `NM_007294.4` as base 114 to base 5,705, with both ends included,
and base 114 is the `A` of the start codon.

Watch what comes back when you hand that 114 to Python without converting it.

```{python}
print(brca1[114])
```

`T`. No error, no complaint, and a perfectly ordinary single base that happens
to belong to the wrong position. The counting started at gap 0, so `brca1[114]`
is the letter after gap 114, which is the 115th letter of the transcript. You
asked for one base and got its neighbor.

Subtract one and try again.

```{python}
print(brca1[113])
```

That `A` is the first base of the start codon, and the two systems now agree
about which letter you meant.

The coding sequence runs to base 5,705, which is well past the 200 bases you
have loaded. Take the first 39 bases of it instead, which is 13 whole codons,
and which is bases 114 to 152 in the record's numbering. Apply rule 2. The
start, 114, becomes 113. The stop, 152, stays at 152.

```{python}
cds_start = brca1[113:152]
print(cds_start)
print(len(cds_start))
```

::: {.check}
Check that 39 two ways, because two routes to one number is the strongest
evidence you can get without anybody to ask. The Python route uses the numbers
in your code: 152 minus 113, which is 39. The record's route uses the numbers
on the record: 152 minus 114 plus 1, which is also 39. They agree here, and
they agree every time the conversion was done right, so a disagreement between
them means one of your two numbers moved when it shouldn't have.
:::

### Why one base matters more here than anywhere else

Bases are read three at a time. A codon is a group of three letters, and the
reading starts at the `A` of `ATG`. Every codon after that gets measured from
there. Slice one base late and every group of three downstream straddles a
boundary that used to sit somewhere else.

```{python}
shifted = brca1[114:153]
print(cds_start[0:3], cds_start[3:6], cds_start[6:9])
print(shifted[0:3], shifted[3:6], shifted[6:9])
```

::: {.trap}
Both of those slices are 39 bases long. Both hold real *BRCA1* sequence. One
reads `ATG GAT TTA` and the other reads `TGG ATT TAT`, and they disagree about
where every codon in the whole coding sequence begins. Chapter 13 turns codons
into a protein. Keep reading in the shifted frame and it runs into `TAG` at
`brca1[177:180]`, which is a stop, while the real frame reads straight past
that spot. Nothing about any of this errors, and the length check you were
relying on passes.
:::

That's the hazard in its purest form. Your slice was one base off, your code
ran, and your output looked exactly like a sequence. The only thing that would
have caught it is knowing that a coding sequence starts with `ATG`.

that cell again if your Colab runtime has restarted since.

::: {.exercise num="11.1" time="20 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Work out the GC content of the first 40 bases of `brca1` on paper, write the
answer down where you can't edit it, and only then run the code.
:::
::: {.given}
The first 40 bases, which are `brca1[0:40]`:

``` {.default}
GCTGAGACTTCCTGGACGGGGGACAGGCTGTGGGGTTTCT
```
:::
::: {.produce}
Four numbers: your hand count of G, your hand count of C, your hand fraction,
and the fraction Python prints. Write the hand numbers down before you type
anything.
:::
::: {.check}
Two invariants catch a miscount. Tally A and T as well, and all four counts
must add to 40. And because the denominator is 40, every correct fraction is a
whole multiple of 0.025, so an answer off by exactly 0.025 means you missed one
base. Then compare your result against the 0.49 you measured across all 200
bases. This window sits ahead of the start codon at base 114 and it comes out
higher, so GC isn't spread evenly even across these 200 bases.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::
:::

at index 114 minus 95 in the string you pulled out. Print those three
characters. If they read `ATG`, both conversions were right. If your `ATG` is
one place to either side, exactly one of your two numbers moved when it
shouldn't have.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str'"}
Python is speaking, and it's telling you that you put quotes around a position.
`brca1["114"]` asks for the letter at position `"114"`, which is text rather
than a number. Drop the quotes: `brca1[114]`. Quotes go around sequence, never
around a position.
:::

::: {.errfix err="IndexError: string index out of range"}
You asked for a letter past the end of the string. `brca1` holds 200
characters, so the last valid index is 199, and `brca1[200]` has nothing to
return. Run `len(brca1)` and check what you're indexing into. A slice behaves
differently here: `brca1[190:400]` gives you whatever exists and raises
nothing, which is convenient and is also how a short answer sneaks past you.
:::

::: {.errfix err="NameError: name 'brca1' is not defined"}
There's no variable by that name in this session. Either the cell that created
`brca1` never ran, or the two spellings differ somewhere. Colab throws away
every variable when the runtime restarts, and the code stays on screen looking
fine while it does. Scroll up and run the first cell again.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your slice runs but the sequence looks wrong"}
Nothing is broken and nothing will tell you. Print the first three characters
of what you extracted. A coding sequence starts with `ATG`, and if yours starts
with `TGG` or `GGA` you're off by one in the direction the trap box above
describes.
:::
:::

:::
